claims.text: The high-temperature mechanical behavior of refractory high-entropy alloys is primarily governed by extensive lattice distortion.
The thermoelastic behavior of refractory high-entropy alloys is primarily governed by extensive lattice distortion.
Extensive lattice distortion pins dislocations and thereby increases yield strength.
Extensive lattice distortion alters phonon modes and thereby reduces thermal expansion.
Significant atomic-size mismatch produces marked lattice distortion in the baseline refractory alloy.
The baseline alloy has a homogeneous single-phase microstructure.
Partial replacement with chemically similar, size-matched elements will reduce lattice distortion.
Local strain fields generated by lattice distortion affect dislocation mobility.
Local strain fields generated by lattice distortion affect phonon behavior.
Reducing lattice distortion lowers the barrier to dislocation motion.
Reducing lattice distortion restores more typical phonon behavior.
Relative to the high-distortion baseline, the reduced-distortion alloy will have lower high-temperature yield strength.
Relative to the high-distortion baseline, the reduced-distortion alloy will have a higher thermal expansion coefficient.
Relative to the high-distortion baseline, the reduced-distortion alloy will show greater dislocation mobility in situ.
The proposed mechanism applies during service-relevant testing from 800°C to 1200°C when oxidation, grain growth, phase instability, and secondary precipitation are controlled.
Chemical short-range ordering or precipitate formation may also influence the measured properties.
